title: Retiring a finance tracker once an agent did the job
summary: I built a household savings tracker by hand, then shut it down when an AI agent covered the need through email and calendar, and I wrote the teardown so the source data survived.

stat.label: an agent working through email and the calendar replaced a hand-built app

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: I had built a private savings and trip tracker over years of bank statements, with its own container, database, public routes and access rules. Then my household's finances moved to an AI agent that works through email and the calendar. It reads the inbox, builds dated bill and payoff events, and checks them the next morning. Nothing in that loop needed a custom app, and I never opened the tracker.
The tracker had become a service with real attack surface and no user. The agent was not a feature on top of it. It made the app unnecessary.

sections.heading: The decision
paragraphs: I weighed what the tracker did that the agent could not. The answer was one thing: hold the source statements. A calendar and an inbox are enough to track due dates and payoffs, and they come with the access controls my household already uses. So I kept the data, and retired the code that served it.
Choosing to remove software because an agent made it redundant is the same judgment as choosing to build it, and I think it is the harder one.

sections.heading: What I built
paragraphs: A teardown in stages, each in code. The first removed the host, the two public routes and their access app, the database, the monitors and the deploy tooling. A second removed the deploy role from the secrets store. A third was a script that deletes the tracker's remaining secrets, and it proves the host is gone before it deletes anything.

The statements were the hard part. Their bucket held the only copy of the source data, so I kept it through the teardown and wrote a separate export script. It copies every object, every older version and every delete marker, then checks each file against the bucket with a hash. It refuses a destination inside any git checkout, so bank data cannot end up in a repository. Removal needs an explicit flag and a typed confirmation, and then it verifies the saved export again instead of copying a second time.

sections.heading: What review found
paragraphs: Two details came out of review. The script treated any message beginning with a common prefix as proof a key was absent, but that prefix appears on every failed lookup, so a broken credential would have looked like a clean removal. It now matches only the exact not-found code. And the storage client reports no latest-version flag, so the inventory records each version's order instead of guessing.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: Stopping a project is a legitimate outcome, and it deserves the same care as shipping one. The same rule from my other work applies: a check that cannot fail is not a check. The teardown treats an unreadable answer as an error, never as absence, and it says what it examined before it reports success.

sources: petedio-iac pull requests for the tracker teardown, the secrets cleanup and the statement export
